title: Search tractability of BLP-solvable promise CSPs
formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite relational structures of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), suppose that the basic linear programming relaxation solves the decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\). Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite input structure \(X\) promised to satisfy \(X\to A\), outputs a homomorphism \(X\to B\)? The algorithm and its polynomial bound may depend on \(A,B\); the promised homomorphism to \(A\) is not supplied.
why: BLP is a central general-purpose tractability criterion for promise constraints. Determining whether its decision power always entails efficient promised search would clarify when an efficiently recognizable relaxation gap can also support construction of the relaxed object. A separation would expose a basic limitation of decision-to-search equivalence even for finite local relations.

sentences: A finite promise CSP asks for weakly satisfying assignments when a strongly satisfying assignment is promised.
BLP can recognize the decision gap using compatible local probability distributions.
The question asks whether every fixed template solved by that relaxation also has a deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm on the original promise.
The algorithm may depend on the template and need not round every feasible point of the relaxation.
A resolution would determine whether this major decision tractability criterion always yields efficient construction of promised solutions.

definitions:
A finite signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^{D}\subseteq D^{r}\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map such that \((d_1,\ldots,d_{r})\in R^{D}\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_{r}))\in R^{E}\) for every relation. It need not be injective. Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists. Templates \(A,B\), including their relation tables and signature, are fixed before inputs are supplied.

An input \(X\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. For a definite encoding, write \(n\) in unary followed by the relation lists in signature order, each prefixed by its tuple count in unary; each coordinate uses exactly \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. The total bit length \(L\) counts isolated variables and all tuples. Duplicate listed tuples are harmless. An output is the list of the \(n\) images in the fixed numbered domain of \(B\), or a distinguished failure symbol. The empty instance has the empty homomorphism.

For each \(x\in X,a\in A\), introduce a rational variable \(p_{x}(a)\). For each constraint \(C=(R,(x_1,\ldots,x_{r}))\) of \(X\) and tuple \(t\in R^{A}\), introduce \(q_{C}(t)\). The basic linear programming relaxation, abbreviated BLP, is feasibility of
\[p_{x}(a)\geq0,\quad \sum_{a\in A}p_{x}(a)=1,\qquad q_{C}(t)\geq0,\quad \sum_{t\in R^{A}}q_{C}(t)=1,\]
\[\sum_{\substack{t\in R^{A}\\t_{i}=a}}q_{C}(t)=p_{x_{i}}(a)\qquad\text{for every }C,\ 1\leq i\leq r,\ a\in A.\]
An empty sum is zero. These conditions are imposed at every coordinate even when a variable repeats in a constraint; no extra constraint forces its coordinates to be equal inside each tuple of a local distribution. Rational and real feasibility coincide for this finite rational system. A homomorphism to \(A\) gives an integral feasible point, but feasibility alone need not give such a homomorphism.

BLP solves the decision problem for \((A,B)\) precisely when, for every finite \(X\), feasibility of the displayed system implies \(X\to B\). This makes feasibility a valid test distinguishing \(X\to A\) from \(X\not\to B\). The search guarantee in the question applies only when \(X\to A\). An input that is BLP-feasible but has no homomorphism to \(A\) is outside that search promise, even though it necessarily has a homomorphism to \(B\).

Polynomial-time search means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no oracle or advice, that halts on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^{k}\) bit steps, for positive integers \(C,k\). On valid promised inputs it returns a \(B\)-homomorphism; on other inputs any output is allowed, and malformed inputs may be rejected. The machine and constants depend only on the fixed template. No common exponent across all templates, algorithm for recognizing BLP-solvable templates, or particular rounding procedure is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish a polynomial-time search machine for every fixed finite BLP-solvable template, with the stated promise, output and worst-case bit bound. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\to B\) satisfying the BLP-solvability hypothesis for which no such polynomial-time promised search machine exists. Difficulty rounding arbitrary feasible LP solutions, undecidability of recognizing templates, or a conditional obstruction to one prescribed algorithm does not prove this negation. An unproved complexity assumption may describe partial progress but does not settle the unconditional target.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP separates a stronger local requirement from a weaker one. Decision only distinguishes instances satisfying all strong constraints from those failing even the weak constraints. Search must actually assign weak-domain values when a strong assignment is guaranteed to exist. This distinction is absent from the familiar fixed-template CSP case, where decision and search are polynomial-time equivalent.

BLP replaces each variable value by a probability distribution and each constraint by a compatible local distribution. Compatibility checks one-variable marginals, so different constraints may agree locally without yielding a joint strong assignment. The BLP-solvability hypothesis guarantees the existence of a weak assignment whenever these local checks succeed; the question asks for a polynomial-time construction on the stronger promise.

The quantifier over fixed templates matters. A separate finite program may use all the information in its particular template, and its polynomial exponent may depend on that template. Consequently, the question is different from recognizing the class of BLP-solvable pairs from their relation tables.

Larrauri’s May 2026 preprint establishes hardness of finding weak assignments for every BLP-accepted input, with reductions from arbitrary total NP search problems. Its discussion explicitly leaves open whether search is tractable on inputs promised to map to the strong template. A total NP search problem has polynomially bounded, polynomially checkable witnesses and at least one witness for every input; its hardness is a statement about this broader input guarantee.
